item.title: OpenAI Pilots Grid Protectors Program at Georgia Compute Campus
item.description:
OpenAI Pilots Grid Protectors Program at Georgia Compute Campus

OpenAI announced it will pilot a “Grid Protectors Program” at an upcoming data center in Effingham County, Georgia. The initiative aims to position its AI data centers—which the company now calls “compute campuses”—as grid resources that can assist power utilities during peak periods and extreme weather events.

🔍 Overview

As public sentiment toward data centers has worsened across the United States, OpenAI is framing its power infrastructure as a protective community resource rather than a polluter. Opposition has mounted nationwide against massive data center developments, which residents report are frequently approved with little or no local input.

⚙️ Key details

  • Grid Protectors Pilot: At its Effingham County, Georgia location, OpenAI promises to free up to 1,000 megawatts of power during emergencies or extreme weather, enough to power air conditioners in around 700,000 homes.
  • Rebranding Efforts: OpenAI has switched to calling its data centers “compute campuses” in an effort to separate from their poor public reputation.
  • Stargate Expansion: OpenAI is partnering with Oracle and SoftBank to build “Stargate” data centers in multiple locations across the country.
  • Utility Arrangements: OpenAI states it will continue working with policymakers and utility services to make arrangements for future campuses to reduce electricity demand when the grid is under strain.

🗺️ Planned OpenAI data center locations

Location Details
Effingham County, Georgia Pilot location for the Grid Protectors Program
Shackelford County, Texas Planned Stargate compute campus with Oracle and SoftBank
Doña Ana County, New Mexico Planned Stargate compute campus with Oracle and SoftBank
Milam County, Texas Planned Stargate compute campus with Oracle and SoftBank

🧩 How it works

OpenAI pitches power plants supplying its compute campuses as resources that utilities can call on when communities need power most. According to OpenAI’s announcement:

  • “Electricity demand also rises and falls with the seasons, with different regions facing their biggest peaks at different times.”
  • “Our compute campuses need power year-round.”
  • “With the right agreements, that steady demand can help spread the grid’s fixed costs across more electricity sales, while flexibility lets us reduce demand when the system is busiest.”

💡 Public opposition and environmental impact

The company’s announcement arrives as community opposition and regulatory scrutiny intensify across several states:

  • Local Protests: In Utah, residents protested after Box Elder County commissioners signed off on a data center expected to consume more than double the state’s peak electricity demand in 2025 and spread hot air into the surrounding desert valley.
  • Air Quality Risks: A study by the Houston Advanced Research Center (HARC) noted that powering proposed Texas data center projects could undo decades of air quality gains over just five years.
  • State Legislation: Several states, including Tennessee, Florida, Oklahoma, and Oregon, have enacted laws to prevent AI companies from passing energy costs on to residents, alongside enacting moratoriums and other restrictions.

#OpenAI #DataCenters #EnergyGrid #Stargate

Source: OpenAI pitches data center power plants as a way to protect nearby areas

item.title: OpenAI Rebrands Data Centers as Compute Campuses Amid Grid Strain Concerns
item.description:
OpenAI Rebrands Data Centers as Compute Campuses Amid Grid Strain Concerns

OpenAI has begun quietly renaming its data centers as “compute campuses” while introducing a new initiative intended to address local power grid concerns. The shift in terminology debuted alongside the announcement of the company’s “Grid Protectors Program.”

🔍 Overview

OpenAI introduced the term “compute campus” in an announcement for its Grid Protectors Program, starting with an upcoming site in Effingham County, Georgia. The initiative aims to address concerns regarding the strain that AI infrastructure puts on local power grids, specifically during emergencies and extreme weather. Axios reported that OpenAI planned to rebrand data centers to “AI compute campuses” as part of a policy and public relations push following the midterm elections in anticipation of potential regulatory hostility.

⚙️ Key details

  • Terminology Shift: Across the roughly 900-word announcement, the term “data center” appeared twice, outnumbered by the new term “compute campus.”
  • Power Commitments: OpenAI promised to “pay the costs we create” and “help communities keep the lights on.”
  • Facility Design: OpenAI stated its new compute facilities differ from older data centers, claiming the new campuses allow the company to remain flexible in power demand.
  • Search History: A search of OpenAI’s website revealed no previous uses of the term “compute campus.”

💡 Critical reception and industry comparison

Critics raised concerns that altering terminology avoids addressing the root issues of infrastructure development. Elmore called the announcement “woefully tone deaf,” stating that changing the name does not solve environmental and climate concerns or fix the issues caused by large construction projects.

Company Infrastructure and Grid Commitments
OpenAI Debuted “compute campus” terminology, launched Grid Protectors Program, and promised flexible power demand and coverage of created costs.
Anthropic Pledged to cover 100 percent of power grid upgrades, invest billions in community projects, protect local water supplies, and refrain from asking public officials to sign NDAs.

OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment regarding its decision to change its terminology or its motivations behind the move.

#OpenAI #DataCenters #EnergyGrid #Anthropic

Source: Midterm elections 2026: all the news Source: OpenAI is quietly renaming data centers ‘compute campuses’

item.title: European Energy Sector Updates Cybersecurity Strategies to Address AI-Driven Grid Threats
item.description:
European Energy Sector Updates Cybersecurity Strategies to Address AI-Driven Grid Threats

Experts gathering at the 9th Cybersecurity Forum in Brussels are warning that the European energy sector must close the gap between rapidly evolving cyber threats and practical response capabilities. The forum addresses new risks created by geopolitical attacks, the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into malicious operations, and the growth of connected energy technologies.

🔍 Overview

The event follows the release of ENISA’s Threat Landscape 2026, which analyzed 8,257 cyber incidents from 2025. The report found that attackers are increasingly incorporating AI into their operations while claims of intrusions related to operational technology (OT)—the systems used to control physical equipment and industrial processes—have increased.

🧩 How it works

The sector is observing how AI can be used as both a tool for attackers and a critical component of grid defense.

Entity AI and Cybersecurity Application
NPC Ukrenergo Uses AI to help cybersecurity teams react faster, identify gaps, support staff, and assist with reporting
Malicious Actors Incorporate AI into operations to shape geopolitical cyber activity and target OT systems
ENCS Identifies vulnerabilities in connected devices that use unauthenticated control protocols

⚙️ Key details

Recent real-world attacks provide a baseline for what grid cyber resilience requires in practice:

  • Poland (December 2025): A coordinated attack targeted wind and solar farms and a combined heat and power plant. Although electricity generation continued, attackers disrupted communications and gained access levels that could have enabled further disruption.
  • Ukraine: NPC Ukrenergo is sharing lessons on maintaining a grid under sustained attack, emphasizing the challenge of keeping specialist cybersecurity expertise when skilled teams are difficult to rebuild.
  • Connected Device Risks: ENCS researchers demonstrated that attackers can use compromised everyday devices, such as routers or cameras, to communicate with residential solar inverters or home batteries that lack command authentication.

💡 Why it matters

The expansion of high-power IoT devices creates a risk where manipulating thousands of units simultaneously could cause sudden changes in generation or demand, potentially leading to wider grid disturbances. Harm van den Brink, a security researcher at ENCS, noted that vulnerabilities in these devices have already been exploited and requires a shift toward independent security testing and manufacturer-led vulnerability management. Dimitra Liveri of ENISA stated that the challenge requires moving from protecting individual systems to optimizing the entire ecosystem for resilience.

#Cybersecurity #ArtificialIntelligence #EnergyGrid #GridResilience #EU

Source: E.DSO, EE-ISAC, ENCS and ENISA 9th Cybersecurity Forum – Press Release | E.DSO
